articles.title: Rochdale holds poignant Remembrance Day services to honour fallen servicemen
articles.excerpt: Thousands gather across the borough to pay their respects during Remembrance Day services, acknowledging the sacrifices made by servicemen and women.
articles.content_html:
Thousands of residents gathered across Rochdale on 8 November 2026 to participate in Remembrance Day services, honouring the sacrifices made by servicemen and women.

The services took place at various memorials throughout the borough, with poignant moments observed as the community came together to remember the fallen.

Elsie Blundell, MP for Heywood and Middleton North, highlighted the importance of these observances, stating that it is crucial to remember those who served.

Rochdale Council acknowledged the significance of the Remembrance Day moment, reinforcing the community's commitment to honouring its heroes. The phrase 'Lest we forget' resonated throughout the ceremonies, reminding attendees of the sacrifices made for their freedom.

These remembrance activities are part of a national observance, reflecting the collective gratitude and respect for those who have served. The turnout at the services demonstrates the community's dedication to remembering its history and the individuals who have shaped it.

articles.title: How many Rochdale servicemen died in the world wars and since? The records give no single answer
articles.excerpt: Between 2,000 and 3,000 Rochdale men are thought to have died in the First World War. No published record gives a borough total for the Second World War or later conflicts.
articles.content_html:
Between 2,000 and 3,000 Rochdale men are thought to have died in the First World War, but no published record gives one total for the borough's war dead.

Rochdale Daily searched the published records on Remembrance Sunday. Different sources give different First World War figures, and none of the sources found gives a borough-wide total for the Second World War or for later conflicts.

First World War

Rochdale Cenotaph, designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens, was unveiled by the Earl of Derby on 26 November 1922. Public subscription raised £29,443 10s, of which £12,611 paid for the memorial. The rest went to a fund for the families of what were then counted as Rochdale's 2,000 war dead.

A later study puts the figure higher. Real Rochdale magazine, marking the centenary in 2018, reported that "approx 3,000 local men died of the 15,000-16,000 who fought in the war", citing Michael Bull's dissertation "Rochdale and the Great War 1914-1920".

The sources do not say whether the two figures cover the same area.

The north face of the Cenotaph reads: "To the memory of the men of Rochdale who gave their lives in the Great War."

Memorial lists are still being corrected. In 2014, seven names were added to Heywood's First World War memorial: W Parkinson, J McIntyre, B C Butterworth, E Collinge, H Armstrong, J Thornley and H Olden. Their links to the town came to light after relatives researched their family trees.

Second World War

The dates 1939-1945 were added to the Cenotaph after the Second World War, and the sunken garden behind it is the borough's Second World War memorial.

No published total for the borough's Second World War dead was found. Smaller records give part of the picture. The war memorial at Rochdale Cemetery lists 54 names from the Second World War, according to the Manchester and Lancashire Family History Society's transcription.

Rochdale Borough Council's list of war dead commemorated at Rochdale Crematorium names 55 service personnel, who died between 1940 and 1947.

Later conflicts

A bronze plaque on the Cenotaph is dedicated "To all those who died in the service of their country".

Corporal Jack Stanley, 26, of The Queen's Royal Hussars, died in April 2012, more than two months after he was injured by an improvised explosive device on patrol near Lashkar Gah in Helmand, Afghanistan. His mother, Brenda, lives in Littleborough.

She said: "Jack was a kind, generous lad with a ready smile." She added: "The world is duller without him and heaven brighter."

Drummer Lee Rigby, 25, of the 2nd Battalion Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, grew up on the Langley estate in Middleton. He was killed near Woolwich Barracks in south-east London in May 2013.

Finding the names

The Commonwealth War Graves Commission's online database lists service personnel who died in both world wars, and the Imperial War Museums' War Memorials Register records the borough's memorials and many of the names on them.

The council publishes lists of war dead buried in eight of the borough's cemeteries and churchyards, including Heywood, Middleton, Rochdale and Littleborough. Families who believe a relative's name is missing from a memorial can contact the council's armed forces team at ArmedForces@rochdale.gov.uk.

The national two-minute silence for Armistice Day takes place at 11am on Wednesday 11 November.

Sources: Rochdale Borough Council; Real Rochdale magazine; Manchester and Lancashire Family History Society; Imperial War Museums; Rochdale Online; Ministry of Defence; Wikipedia's entry on Rochdale Cenotaph. Photograph: Rochdale Borough Council.

articles.title: Asda worker Saheda Bibi praised for supporting widowed customer in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Saheda Bibi, an Asda employee in Rochdale, has been recognised for her kindness in helping a recently widowed customer with her shopping needs.
articles.content_html:
An Asda employee in Rochdale has received praise for her compassionate support of a recently widowed customer. Saheda Bibi, 43, has worked at the store since 2012 and made a promise to look after the woman after learning about her loss.

The customer’s daughter, who lives in London, expressed concern about how her mother would manage alone following her husband's death. Saheda reassured her by sharing her work schedule, allowing the daughter to plan her mother's shopping trips accordingly.

Since then, Saheda has assisted the woman with her shopping, ensuring she has a chair to sit on and taking the time to chat with her.

The customer was so grateful for Saheda's kindness that she contacted the store's customer manager, Dave Jeffs, to express her appreciation.

In recognition of her outstanding service, Dave has nominated Saheda for an Asda Service Superstar Award, highlighting the positive impact she has made on the customer's life during a difficult time.

articles.title: Rochdale Council leaves door open for Hopwood Hall reconciliation after court ruling
articles.excerpt: Following a recent High Court ruling, Rochdale Council has expressed willingness to engage with filmmaker Hopwood DePree regarding the future of Hopwood Hall, which has been a point of contention since the termination of their agreement in 2024.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has indicated a willingness to engage in discussions with filmmaker Hopwood DePree regarding the future of Hopwood Hall, following a recent High Court ruling that upheld the council's decision to terminate their agreement.

This development comes after a two-day trial at Manchester Civil Justice Centre in September, where the court ruled that the council acted lawfully in ending the exclusivity agreement with DePree, who had sought to purchase the historic site for £1.

The council's option agreement with DePree, which began in 2017, was terminated in October 2024, leading to a legal dispute. DePree, who claims ancestral ties to the hall, believed he had a binding agreement to purchase the property.

However, the court found that a planning approval granted in 2022 did not trigger the option to buy the hall for the nominal fee.

In response to the court's decision, DePree has issued an open letter to the council, outlining his terms for a potential resolution.

He expressed a desire for constructive dialogue and transparency regarding the council's decisions, including a request for the release of documents related to the handling of the hall's management. DePree has suggested that an independent review could help clarify the situation and facilitate discussions.

Council leader Neil Emmott reiterated that the council's 'door is always open' for DePree to present a viable plan for Hopwood Hall's future.

Both parties have acknowledged that the costly court battle could have been avoided, and there is hope for an amicable resolution that benefits the community and preserves the historic site.

articles.title: Heywood lollipop man forced to leap out of way as drivers ignore crossing
articles.excerpt: A car and a moped have been seized after their drivers failed to stop for a lollipop man in Heywood, forcing him to jump aside for safety.
articles.content_html:
A car and a moped have been seized by Greater Manchester Police after their drivers ignored a lollipop man in Heywood, forcing him to leap out of the way on two separate occasions. The incidents occurred on Bury Old Road on 13 and 14 October, as reported by Rochdale Borough Council.

Barry Jones, the lollipop man involved, was standing in the road when both vehicles failed to stop. The council noted that there have been 137 reported incidents of drivers not stopping for school crossing patrols across the borough in the last five years, highlighting a concerning trend regarding road safety near schools.

Following the incidents, police gathered evidence, including witness statements, which led to the seizure of the silver Skoda car and the moped.

A recent change in law, effective from June, allows police to seize vehicles without issuing a warning first under the Police Reform Act 2002.

Dylan Williams, the cabinet member for highways, expressed gratitude to the police for their prompt action and stated that the council would continue to report such incidents and pursue prosecutions where possible.

Thirty-four foster families were honoured at the annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards held at Rochdale Town Hall, recognising their dedication to providing safe and nurturing homes for vulnerable children.

Collectively, these families have fostered for an impressive 465 years, supporting over 1,020 children and young people from newborns to 18 years old.

Marilyn expressed her love for fostering, stating, "How long is a piece of string?" when asked how long they would continue. She reflected on the joy of seeing children grow up and receiving letters from adoptive parents thanking them for their influence.

The event highlighted the vital role foster families play in the community, providing stability and care to those in need. The awards serve not only to recognise the individual contributions of these families but also to raise awareness about the importance of fostering in Rochdale.

With many children still in need of stable homes, the event aims to inspire others in the community to consider fostering.

For those interested in becoming foster carers, further information can be obtained from the local authority's fostering service.

articles.content_html:
Foster carers in Milnrow were recently honoured for their remarkable collective service of 465 years at an awards ceremony held by Rochdale Borough Council. The event celebrated the commitment and dedication of these individuals who have provided care and support to children in need.

Among those recognised were Michael and Marilyn, who have fostered children for an impressive 50 years. Their long-standing service has made a significant impact on the lives of many children, and they have attended numerous events celebrating the achievements of those they have fostered.

Marilyn expressed her desire to continue fostering, highlighting the joy and fulfilment it brings to their lives.

The ceremony included heartfelt letters from adoptive parents, expressing gratitude for the care and support provided by the foster carers.

These testimonials underscored the vital role that foster carers play in the community and the positive influence they have on the lives of children and families.

The council encourages anyone interested in becoming a foster carer to reach out and learn more about the process, as there is always a need for dedicated individuals to provide loving homes for children.

Between all the carers, it is estimated they have supported more than 1,020 children and young people from newborn to 18, while working with the local authority. Among those celebrating their individual milestones was Michael, aged 79, and Marilyn, aged 75, who are marking an incredible 50 years. Predominantly caring for newborn babies and siblings since 1976, the married couple from Milnrow have cared for more than 330 children in that time with no signs yet of them slowing down. “How long is a piece of string?” Marilyn joked when asked how long she will continue to foster for, before adding she would really miss fostering. Another couple who have kindly dedicated their lives to providing a safe and stable home to those who need it the most, is Carole, aged (65) and Ian (67) McLean from Rochdale, who are celebrating 40 years. Looking back at their own experience as foster carers, Ian said: “When the children do go, they always take something with them of us because we give them that stability, assistance and support. “We even give them support when they’ve gone and we’ve got a number of former foster children that we class as family and they call us mum and dad, I’ve even given 2 of them away at their weddings.” Among many more memorable moments they have shared as foster carers, Carole was also the birthing partner to another former foster child, an experience she simply described as being ‘brilliant’ to be a part of. "Whether they have been fostering for a few years or several decades, each and every one of them has helped provide the stability, care and support that children need to thrive. “On behalf of Rochdale Borough Council, I would like to thank all our foster carers for the life-changing contribution they make to our communities." articles.title: £150 off energy bills: Rochdale households urged to watch for important letter
articles.excerpt: Warm Home Discount confirmation letters are arriving for eligible households, with the £150 energy credit applied over the winter rather than paid to everyone at once.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale residents who qualify for £150 off their energy bills are being urged to check their post as Warm Home Discount confirmation letters begin arriving.

The government started issuing letters on Thursday, 22 October, with correspondence continuing through to January 2027.

Around six million households across Britain are expected to benefit this winter. The letters will explain whether the discount will be applied automatically or whether the recipient needs to provide more information.

Anyone whose letter asks them to contact the Warm Home Discount helpline must do so before 26 February 2027.

The Warm Home Discount supports eligible households, including people receiving qualifying means tested benefits. Eligibility depends on the scheme’s rules, including benefit entitlement and the electricity account arrangements on the qualifying date.

For this winter, the qualifying date was 23 August 2026.

The £150 is normally applied directly to an eligible household’s electricity account. It is not a cash payment into a bank account, and there is no single payment day for everyone in Rochdale.

Eligible customers should receive their discount by 31 March 2027. Residents can check their supplier’s app, online account or bill for the credit.

The scheme is separate from the Winter Fuel Payment and Cold Weather Payments. Receiving the Warm Home Discount does not affect either entitlement.

For households watching every pound, the important step is to read the letter carefully and respond if action is requested.

Have you received your letter or seen the £150 appear on your energy account? Tell us your supplier and experience in the comments, keeping account numbers and personal details private.

articles.title: Rochdale Council generates nearly £3 million from parking fines over three years
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has collected £2.88 million from parking fines since 2023, with funds reinvested into local road infrastructure.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has reported a total of £2.88 million generated from parking fines over the last three years, according to data obtained through a Freedom of Information request. This figure represents an average of just under £1 million per year from 2023 to 2026, with the highest earnings recorded in 2025, amounting to £990,256.

In total, the council issued 90,644 parking charge notices (PCNs) during this period. The overall value of these notices exceeded £5.6 million; however, the actual income is lower due to successful challenges against fines and the costs associated with enforcement.

The council has stated that all revenue from PCNs is reinvested into the local road network, which may include repairs to potholes, repainting road markings, and funding larger infrastructure projects.

The council emphasised that PCNs are issued not only for revenue generation but also for safety reasons, such as ensuring adequate space for wheelchair users on pavements and preventing blind spots at junctions.

The data also highlighted the busiest areas for parking fines, with Newgate, Yorkshire Street Central, and Oldham Road Central identified as the top hotspots for PCNs issued.

This financial strategy raises questions about the balance between enforcement and community needs, as residents may feel the impact of increased parking restrictions.

articles.title: M6 Theatre receives £73,500 funding for 50th anniversary project
articles.excerpt: M6 Theatre in Rochdale has been awarded £73,500 to support its 50th anniversary project, which will include community outreach and an interactive exhibition.
articles.content_html:
M6 Theatre, a prominent institution in Rochdale, has been awarded £73,500 to fund its upcoming 50th anniversary project, set to take place in 2027.

This funding will support a range of initiatives aimed at celebrating the theatre's rich history and its impact on the community over the past five decades.

The anniversary project will feature an interactive exhibition and a digital archive, allowing audiences to engage with the theatre's legacy. M6 Theatre plans to conduct community outreach projects that will collect stories from individuals who have been involved with the theatre throughout its history.

This initiative aims to highlight the journeys of both audiences and theatre professionals.

Founded in 1977, M6 Theatre has made a significant impact on the lives of over 500,000 children and young people through its touring theatre productions.

The anniversary celebrations will include a new youth theatre show, a community gala, and the commissioning of a specially made film and poem, all designed to enhance public accessibility and involvement.

The project will unfold over the course of one year, culminating in a celebration of M6 Theatre's contributions to the arts and education in the region.

articles.title: Urgent appeal to find woman after suspected human tissue discovered in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Police fear a woman who may have recently given birth needs urgent medical attention after a discovery near Watkins Street and Charter Street, off Kingsway.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS | ONGOING AND DEVELOPING STORY. This report will be updated when further verified information becomes available.

Detectives are trying to find a woman who may need urgent medical attention after suspected human tissue was discovered off Kingsway in Rochdale.

Greater Manchester Police said evidence found near the junction of Watkins Street and Charter Street suggests a woman may have recently given birth. Officers were called shortly before 9am on Thursday 22 October.

Police have been examining the scene and carrying out enquiries. Their priority is to find the woman and make sure she is safe and well.

Detective Inspector Daniel Daly, from GMP's Rochdale CID, said: “She may be in need of urgent medical attention, and she is our absolute priority at the moment - that is why we are asking anyone with information to contact us.”

Anyone with information, or who may have seen a woman in distress, should call 101 and quote incident number 684 of 22/10/2026.

Information can also be reported online or through GMP's LiveChat service at https://www.gmp.police.uk. Alternatively, contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

DI Daly asked the public not to speculate: “We would ask that people don't speculate on the circumstances of this discovery as it hinders our investigation and is upsetting for those involved.”

The information in this report comes from Greater Manchester Police's appeal issued on 22 October 2026. Police have not confirmed further circumstances in that appeal.

Jawad Ali, 20, reported that a woman became aggressive and shouted racial slurs at a black security guard when asked to move away from an exit.

The incident, captured on video and shared widely online, shows the woman making derogatory gestures towards the guard. Ali, who was working for Protective One Security at the time, described the behaviour as "disgusting" and stated that he now expects such incidents during his shifts.

Greater Manchester Police confirmed they have received a report regarding the incident and are currently conducting inquiries. Ali alleged that the woman also directed racial abuse towards him before the video was recorded.

This incident raises significant concerns about the treatment of security staff and the prevalence of racial abuse in nightlife settings. As investigations continue, it highlights the need for greater awareness and action against such behaviour.

articles.title: Rochdale schools benefit from Tesco's Free Fruit and Veg programme
articles.excerpt: Schools across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale, received over 750,000 portions of fruit and vegetables through Tesco's initiative, promoting healthier eating among pupils.
articles.content_html:
Schools across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale, have received a total of 750,600 portions of fruit and vegetables as part of Tesco's Free Fruit & Veg for Schools programme. This initiative, now in its third year, aims to encourage healthier eating habits among children.

The produce, which weighed more than 60,000 kilograms, was distributed to schools throughout the region. Apples were the most popular choice, with approximately 221,000 portions consumed, followed by bananas at around 103,000 portions. Satsumas and clementines also featured prominently, with about 88,000 portions provided.

Since its launch, the programme has supplied nearly 20 million portions of fruit and vegetables across the UK, benefiting up to 186,000 pupils.

According to a recent impact report, 98% of teachers reported that the initiative encouraged students to try a wider variety of fruits, while 94% noted improvements in student behaviour.

While specific figures for Rochdale schools were not disclosed, the overall success of the programme highlights its positive impact on children's nutrition and well-being. As the scheme continues, it is expected to reach even more schools and students in the coming year.

The youngster said: “I saw my dad playing the guitar and I thought it really sounded cool, and then I wanted to give it a try. Adrian prepares for his first live performance. Adrian said: “My favourite song would be Eruption from Van Halen, and since I just really like the tapping pod and it just really gets me. Abraham said: “When people hear Adrian, a lot of them want him in a band, but by the time they see him, they’re like, he’s too little . . . his guitar is taller than him!” But Adrian is clear that music will be in his future. He said: “My dream would be to be the best guitarist in the world and be playing with famous bands and having fun with them too.” But playing the guitar has other benefits too. He added: “I usually just like it because it sounds good, it comes down my stress and it helps me play it and it helps me to just enjoy relax and play some good songs because usually most of the songs are heavy metal.” By sharing his journey on Instagram, Adrian and Abraham want to inspire others to do the same. You can do it anytime, and you can’t, if Adrian can do it, so can you.” He joked: “I’ve got a daughter as well now she she’s only four years old, but she’s picked up the guitar because she thinks that’s the only way to get attention in the house!” Adrian and his dad, Abraham. articles.title: St Cuthbert’s evacuated as message reassures parents all children and staff are safe
articles.excerpt: St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust says St Cuthbert’s was evacuated following a possible bomb threat. All children and staff are safe; parents can collect pupils.
articles.content_html:
Latest update — St Teresa of Calcutta trust statement

St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, which oversees St Cuthbert’s RC High School, has released a statement saying staff received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat on Friday morning, 16 October.

The trust says emergency services were called, all school buildings were evacuated as a precaution and Greater Manchester Police attended. All children and staff are safe and accounted for, it says.

Parents and carers can now collect their children or give consent for them to travel home, according to the statement. The trust says specialist security operatives will carry out a full sweep of the building this afternoon. It currently expects the school to reopen as normal on Monday 19 October, subject to further updates.

The trust’s account conflicts with some earlier reports circulating about the incident. In particular, it describes rumours of intruders or weapons on school premises as false. Earlier references to a lockdown should be read alongside this latest statement, which describes a precautionary evacuation following a possible bomb threat.

This remains a developing story. Rochdale Daily will continue to update this article with official information as it is released. The earlier updates below are retained for context; the latest trust statement takes precedence where accounts differ.

Trust statement in full:

Earlier this morning (Friday 16 October 2026), staff at St. Cuthbert's RC High School in Rochdale received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat to the premises.

The emergency services were called and all school buildings were evacuated as a precautionary measure.

All children and staff are safe and accounted for, in line with our established procedures.

Greater Manchester Police attended and parents and carers were notified immediately that their children had been removed to a safe distance and there was no threat or danger to anyone present.

We would like to assure everyone within the St Cuthbert’s School community that the safety and wellbeing of our children remains our absolute priority.

Specialist security operatives will conduct a full sweep of the building this afternoon to confirm if any further actions are required.

Currently, the expectation is that the school will be open as normal on Monday 19 October - but further information will be communicated as needed when received.

Parents and carers can now attend the school to collect their children, or provide consent for their children to travel home.

We’d like to thank parents, carers and colleagues for their understanding and co-operation in this matter.

We’d also urge people to avoid speculation on social media - particularly regarding false rumours, such as any referring to intruders or weapons being present on school premises.

More details will be communicated when appropriate, following consultation with GMP and Rochdale Borough Council.

Source: Statement attributed to St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, supplied to Rochdale Daily on 16 October 2026.

Earlier updates — before the trust statement

Developing update — councillor requests official briefing

Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short has said he is urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police following reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School. In a statement supplied to Rochdale Daily, he said he first learned of the reports through the Manchester Evening News and had not received an official briefing.

His statement does not establish what prompted the incident. The earlier message shared with Rochdale Daily described a precautionary evacuation and said all children and staff were safe and accounted for.

Councillor Tarrant-Short’s statement in full:

I want to address the reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School.

First and foremost, my thoughts are with the children, their families and the staff. I understand how frightening this situation will be, particularly for parents waiting for information and reassurance.

I want to be clear: I first became aware of this through the Manchester Evening News. I have not received an official briefing.

I am now urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police so I can understand what has happened and what support is being provided to those affected.

Having been through a similar situation myself when Newhouse Academy went into lockdown, I know how distressing that uncertainty can feel. Behind every update are children who may be frightened and families desperate to know their loved ones are safe.

I am asking that communication with families is timely, clear and compassionate, and that support is available for anyone left distressed.

Until there is verified information, I will not speculate about the circumstances. Please follow official updates from the school and police, and avoid sharing rumours.

The immediate priority must be the safety and wellbeing of every child and member of staff.

Earlier report

St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale has been evacuated as a precaution, according to a message to parents and carers shared with Rochdale Daily.

The message states: “All children and staff are safe and accounted for.”

It reassures families that pupils’ safety and wellbeing remain the school’s “absolute priority” and says staff are managing the situation in line with established procedures.

Parents and carers have been told they will receive another communication as soon as further information is available.

The message does not explain what prompted the evacuation or give instructions for collecting children.

St Cuthbert’s is on Shaw Road in Rochdale. The school’s website is https://www.stcuthberts.stoccat.org.uk/.

This is a developing story.

articles.title: Rochdale Council plans major investments and heritage restoration
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has announced significant investments in heritage restoration and community services, including plans for Hopwood Hall and Middleton's regeneration projects, aimed at boosting local economy and services.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has outlined a series of major investments aimed at revitalising the borough, with a focus on heritage restoration and community services. In a recent column, Councillor Neil Emmott highlighted the council's commitment to enhancing local infrastructure and supporting residents amid ongoing cost-of-living challenges.

A key development is the council's recent victory in the High Court regarding Hopwood Hall, a historic building in Middleton. The ruling provides clarity on the future of the site, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. Plans for essential repairs and feasibility studies are underway, with the aim of restoring the hall to serve the community and preserve its historical significance.

In addition to Hopwood Hall, the council is advancing its regeneration plans for Middleton. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to attract a new tenant by the end of the year, while the long-derelict Warwick Mill is also set for redevelopment, potentially including new housing. Furthermore, the transformation of the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue is in progress, aimed at providing activities and training for young people.

These initiatives are part of a broader strategy to stimulate economic growth and create jobs across the borough.

With banking and post office services returning to Middleton town centre in the new year, local leaders are optimistic about the positive impact these developments will have on the community.

articles.title: Court Rules on Ownership Dispute Over Hopwood Hall
articles.excerpt: A High Court ruling has denied Hopwood DePree's claim to ownership of Hopwood Hall, concluding that Rochdale Council acted fairly in its decision to end the exclusivity agreement.
articles.content_html:
A High Court in Manchester has ruled against Hopwood DePree in his bid to gain ownership of Hopwood Hall, a historic manor house in Rochdale. The ruling concluded that Rochdale Council acted fairly when it ended an exclusivity agreement with DePree, who is a descendant of the family that originally built the hall in the 1420s.

The two-day trial, which concluded on 20 October 2026, centred on DePree's claim that the council had reneged on an agreement allowing him to purchase the Grade II-listed property. The council had previously worked with DePree for seven years to facilitate repairs on the dilapidated site, which is now part of Hopwood Hall College. However, in November 2024, the council stated it would explore other options, citing a lack of a commercially viable business model from DePree.

Following the court's decision, DePree expressed disappointment, stating that the ruling was a significant setback for both his family and the community. He indicated that he and his legal team are considering their options moving forward, while also pledging to monitor the council's efforts to restore the hall for public benefit.

Hopwood Hall has a rich history, having been owned by the Hopwood family until 1922, after which it changed hands several times and fell into disrepair. The council acquired the property in the 1980s and has since been responsible for its maintenance.

articles.title: High Court rules against filmmaker in Hopwood Hall restoration dispute
articles.excerpt: A recent High Court ruling has concluded a legal battle between American filmmaker Hopwood DePree and Rochdale Council over the future of Hopwood Hall in Middleton.
articles.content_html:
A High Court ruling has determined that American filmmaker Hopwood DePree does not have the right to purchase Hopwood Hall, a Grade-II* listed building in Middleton, following a protracted legal dispute with Rochdale Council. The decision was announced during a hearing at the Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, marking a significant setback for DePree, who has invested over £750,000 in efforts to restore the historic estate.

The saga began in 2017 when DePree signed an options agreement with the council to lead the redevelopment of Hopwood Hall. His vision included transforming the 1400s stately home into a wedding and hospitality venue, complete with a hotel retreat, gift shop, and guided tours.

DePree engaged the local community in his restoration efforts, which included extensive work on the hall's gardens and interior.

Before DePree's involvement, Hopwood Hall had fallen into disrepair, with its last known use being as part of De La Salle College, which closed in 1989.

The hall had previously served as a venue for various events, including an underground bar and nightclub during the 1960s and 70s, where notable acts such as Black Sabbath performed.

The ruling concludes a decade-long effort by DePree to revive the hall, which has been under the ownership of Rochdale Council since the college's closure. The future of Hopwood Hall now remains uncertain as the council considers its next steps regarding the estate.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The Hopwood Hall saga | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The Hopwood Hall saga George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 10, 2026 | 8:44 AM Print The Grade-II listed Hopwood Hall in Middleton When an American filmmaker and Rochdale council signed an agreement over a shared ambition to restore Hopwood Hall, no one could have fathomed the furious saga that unfolded. What started as a harmonious relationship between Hopwood DePree and the local authority ended up with them being on opposite sides of a court room. Mr DePree claims ancestral connections to the Grade-II* listed building in Middleton. His dream was to bring the 1400s stately home back to life. He even roped in the local community to help him do it, apparently spending more than £750,000 on the project. On what he described as a ‘sad day’ in Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, his dream was crushed. The High Court ruled in favour of the council following a legal battle over whether Mr DePree had the right to buy the estate or not. The saga began in 2017 when Hopwood DePree signed an options agreement with town hall bosses to lead the redevelopment of the hall. Since then he has led a decade-long community effort to do exactly that. The Hollywood man’s vision saw the hall transformed into a wedding and hospitality venue, with a hotel ‘retreat’, gift shop and guided tours all part of the package. His team could regularly be seen working on the hall’s gardens and titivating the interior in the years since. Before Mr DePree came along, the hall had fallen into disrepair and irrelevance. Its last known use was as part of the De La Salle College, which shut down in 1989. During the 1960s and 70s it was said to be the setting for an underground bar and nightclub. It is believed that Ozzy Osbourne’s band Black Sabbath and other iconic performers played there. Since the closure of the college, the hall has been in the possession of Rochdale council. The American even created a Youtube series and wrote a book about his journey refurbishing what he affectionately called ‘Downton Shabby’. However, this journey came to an abrupt halt when the council ended the agreement in October 2024 and, without warning, barred Mr DePree and his group from the building. Part of the options agreement allowed the US actor and producer to purchase the historic asset from landowners Rochdale council for a ‘peppercorn fee’ – £1. Mr DePree attempted to exercise that option the day before the council ended the agreement, which was denied by town hall chiefs. Since then, a two-year-long war of words has raged between Mr DePree and Rochdale council. The American threatened legal action for months, but the council never budged. Mr DePree believed the local authority acted unlawfully by denying his ‘legally binding’ option to buy Hopwood Hall. At the time, the council said they ended the agreement because Mr DePree hadn’t made enough progress with the restoration effort. This expulsion from the estate came following a number of extensions to the agreement made by the council. The local authority even granted ‘change of use’ planning permission to Mr DePree for Hopwood Hall in 2022. Until the two sides decided to settle the matter in High Court, it was unclear just how important that planning permission was. Effectively, approved planning permission was the trigger to open up the option for Mr DePree to have the estate transferred to him. The High Court played host to Hopwood Hall Estate Ltd vs Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council this week. In the words of Mr DePree’s barrister, Ashley Bowes, the planning permission was ‘the star of the show’. The court heard details of the dispute over whether Mr DePree had authority to trigger the transfer of the property based on the approved plans. The council’s barrister Geraint Wheatley said the plans did not go far enough in demonstrating a serious commitment to reinstate and refurbish the 1400s building, as required by the options agreement. He described the ‘ruined’ hall as needing far more than some internal works to bring it back to a state of habitation. According to Mr Wheatley the conditions of the options agreement to trigger the purchase of the hall had four elements – authorisation to reinstate and refurbish the building; agreed standard of refurbishment between the parties (fit for habitation); English Heritage approval; and that the property would be reinstated and refurbished in whole, not in part. The defence barrister pointed out that getting permission for events and hospitality space for part of the ground floor doesn’t relate to the building ‘in whole’, as requested in the agreement clause. He also pointed out that the plans wouldn’t have seen the hall be fit for habitation or reinstated and refurbished. “Obtaining a mere ‘change of use’ permission doesn’t show a great deal of commitment,” Mr Wheatley told the court. “Plans of physical work show that commitment.” Mr Wheatley also tried to argue that English Heritage approval wasn’t given. But His Honour Judge Hodge KC believed the organisation’s support for the 2022 plans qualified as their approval. Buoyed by the judge agreeing with one point of the claimant, Dr Bowes said the 2022 application was internal work that would have created an events and hospitality space and enabled future work to be reinstated and refurbished. He said the claimant didn’t think anything more than a change of use application would be necessary to trigger the purchase as it wasn’t specified in the agreement. Dr Bowes said it was ‘wishful thinking’ on the council’s part that a community group would spend huge sums of money drawing up plans for physical works when they didn’t think it would be necessary. After delving into detailed planning legislation; the interpretation of wording in the agreement; and the cross-examinations of both Hopwood DePree and council boss for economy and place, Mark Robinson, the judge ruled in favour of the defendant – Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council. His Honour Judge Hodge KC described how the planning application did not cover the whole of the property or showcase the ability to reinstate and refurbish Hopwood Hall, as required in the options agreement. He added: “I am satisfied, for the reasons I have given, that the planning permission does not satisfy the requirements of the options agreement. I therefore refuse to grant the relief sought by the claimant.” A lengthy saga was ended by a two-day trial. Instead of getting Hopwood Hall for £1, Mr DePree was landed with a £114,000 bill to cover the council’s court costs. However, the American said the fight isn’t over and Hopwood Hall ‘must be saved’. He didn’t confirm whether his team would appeal the judgement, but they have until November 18 to do so. Speaking after the case, Mr DePree said: “Obviously I am incredibly disappointed. Not just me but the community of support around the world and the UK charitable groups as well. “I am already discussing with my legal team about the next steps. In the meantime I hope Rochdale council will be watching over Hopwood Hall because we will be keeping an eye on them. “We are not giving up. Hopwood Hall must be saved. In the two years we have been locked out the gardens have gone into wrack and ruin. I hope they will step up and save the hall. I still think the community group and I are the best people to take this forward. “I am getting messages from around the world with people offering money and support. It is a sad day but we will have to have a look at our options.” The town hall has committed to maintaining the building and have commissioned a feasibility study to look into possible future uses for the historic asset. A Rochdale council spokesperson said: “We are pleased with today’s judgement. It’s a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested into this process could have been better spent on the hall itself. “We’re now focussed on moving forward. More than £1.6m has been spent on the hall by ourselves and Historic England since 2017 and we will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. Feasibility studies have already been completed and options for Hopwood Hall’s long-term future will be considered in due course. “One thing we are clear on is, whatever the future holds for Hopwood Hall, this building, once restored and refurbished, will be used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton’s rich and varied heritage.” Add Roch Valley Radio as a preferred source on Google News to see more of our local reporting Add as a preferred source on Google Do you have a story for us? articles.title: Rochdale's music heritage celebrated in New album 'Kenion Street'
articles.excerpt: The album 'Kenion Street', believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council, showcases local talent and pays tribute to the town's rich musical history.
articles.content_html:
An album titled 'Kenion Street', believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council, has gained significant attention, reaching millions of listeners on national radio and streaming platforms.

Launched as part of Rochdale's year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture, the album features local artists performing reimagined versions of classic tracks recorded at the town's iconic studios.

From 1977 to 2001, Rochdale was home to Suite Sixteen and Cargo Studios, located on Kenion Street, where renowned artists such as OMD, The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Joy Division, and Inspiral Carpets recorded some of their most memorable work.

The album includes 11 tracks, featuring PoolEra's rendition of OMD's 'Electricity', Medley's version of New Order's 'Dreams Never End', and Jennifer Read's interpretation of The Fall's 'Totally Wired'.

All tracks were recorded and produced at Voltalab Sound Studios, situated in the original Cargo/Suite Sixteen building, by studio founder Jamie Alsop. The album has received positive reviews and was featured on Radio 6 Music, where Middleton band K-Estate's cover of Gang of Four's 'Damaged Goods' was highlighted as Track of the Day. Other tracks have been played across various stations, including XS Manchester and Mersey Radio, reaching a combined audience of over 3.5 million.

The release of 'Kenion Street' not only showcases local talent but also serves as a reminder of Rochdale's significant contribution to the music industry.

articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Police has launched an urgent appeal to find 10-year-old Rayah, who was last seen on Bower Avenue in Rochdale at around 8.30am today.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester Police has launched an urgent appeal to find 10-year-old Rayah, who has been missing from Rochdale since this morning.

Rayah was last seen on Bower Avenue in Rochdale at around 8.30am on Friday 14 August. Police say officers are becoming increasingly concerned about her and want to make sure she is safe and well.

The police appeal describes Rayah as a child with olive or tanned skin, approximately 4ft 5in tall, with mousey brown curly hair worn in a ponytail.

She was last seen wearing purple and white striped bottoms, a T-shirt and a denim jacket. She was also carrying a backpack and had a remote-control car with her.

Anyone who sees Rayah, knows where she may be, or has information which could help officers locate her is urged to contact Greater Manchester Police on 0161 856 1367, quoting reference MSP/06PP/0001322/26.

Always call 999 in an emergency.

The Summit Inn has reopened its doors with a new menu packed with traditional pub favourites, homemade dishes and lighter lunch options.

The new menu combines familiar pub dishes with several homemade elements and gives customers options ranging from a bowl of soup or sandwich through to a more substantial lunch.

articles.title: Norden residents report being without water since Friday morning as outage continues
articles.excerpt: Residents in Norden say they have been without water since around 9am on Friday, with households reporting an extended loss of supply and frustration over the apparent lack of an on-site response.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Norden are reporting that they have been without running water since around 9am on Friday, with the disruption continuing into Saturday and households asking when their supply will return.

Rochdale Daily has received reports from residents describing a prolonged loss of supply and saying they have seen no sign of United Utilities teams in their immediate area. At the time of publication, Rochdale Daily has not independently confirmed the cause, the precise number of properties affected or an estimated restoration time.

The length of the reported interruption is significant. United Utilities' published standards say that where a burst on one of its pipes causes an unexpected loss of supply, it aims to restore water within 12 hours. The company says that where it identifies that it has failed to restore supply within 12 hours, household customers should automatically receive £50, plus another £50 for each additional 12-hour period they remain without water. Eligibility will depend on the circumstances of the interruption and the company's standards.

WHAT SHOULD RESIDENTS DO?

Anyone still without water should report the problem directly to United Utilities, even if neighbours have already done so. Its 24-hour water and wastewater number is 0345 672 3723. Residents can also use the United Utilities website to check for active incidents affecting their postcode and report water-supply problems.

If neighbouring properties have water but yours does not, United Utilities advises carrying out basic household checks. The internal stop tap, commonly located beneath the kitchen sink, can be turned off and back on several times while the cold kitchen tap is running, which may clear an airlock or obstruction. If an entire street or neighbourhood is affected, the problem is more likely to be on the wider network and should be reported to the company.

Residents should keep a record of when their supply stopped, any reference numbers given by United Utilities, screenshots of incident updates and details of calls or messages. This may be useful if the interruption later qualifies for a standards-of-service payment or if a complaint needs to be escalated.

VULNERABLE RESIDENTS AND BOTTLED WATER

People who are older, disabled, have medical needs, mobility difficulties, young children at home or otherwise need additional support should tell United Utilities immediately and ask about its free Priority Services scheme.

United Utilities says that if water is likely to remain off for more than 12 hours it will try to make alternative supplies available in the affected area. Priority Services customers who cannot collect alternative supplies may be able to receive bottled water at home.

Priority Services can be contacted on 0345 072 6093. United Utilities' published Priority Services commitments also include bottled-water support during qualifying prolonged emergency interruptions, with enhanced arrangements for its most vulnerable customers.

Residents who rely on water for home dialysis or another essential medical treatment should make this clear when contacting the company rather than waiting for a general area update.

If United Utilities confirms an alternative bottled-water collection point, Rochdale Daily will add the location to this story.

WHAT ABOUT COMPENSATION?

United Utilities' current standards of service state that an unexpected mains interruption lasting beyond 12 hours can trigger an automatic £50 payment, followed by a further £50 for each additional 12-hour period without water where the relevant standard applies. Residents should therefore retain evidence of the duration of the outage and check subsequent bills or correspondence.

If an eligible payment is not made, customers can raise the matter directly with United Utilities through its complaints process.

Rochdale Daily has sought further information on the cause of the Norden disruption, the number of properties affected, what work is under way, whether alternative water supplies are being provided and when residents can expect normal service to return.

This is a developing story and will be updated as further verified information becomes available.

articles.title: Are Facebook Groups Becoming the Gatekeepers of Local News?
articles.excerpt: Large community Facebook groups now play a major role in determining which local stories residents see, raising questions about moderation, access to information and the influence of digital gatekeepers.
articles.content_html:
Recent posts from independent local news publishers have, at times, remained pending approval or failed to appear in large community Facebook groups. The reasons are not always clear and may range from routine moderation and administrative delays to editorial decisions made by group administrators.

Whatever the explanation, the situation raises a wider question about how much influence large local Facebook groups have over the news and viewpoints residents are exposed to.

Many of these groups have memberships larger than the circulation of traditional local newspapers. For thousands of people, they have become the primary place where local news, events and community discussion are discovered. Decisions about which posts are approved can therefore have a significant impact on what information reaches the public.

Independent journalism exists to report what is happening within a community, regardless of whether those stories are politically convenient or uncomfortable. It should not matter whether a story reflects positively or negatively on any political party, campaign group or public body. The role of journalism is to inform readers, not to tell them what to think.

Equally, moderation is an important part of running any online community. Administrators are entitled to remove unlawful material, spam, abuse, hate speech or defamatory content. However, where lawful reporting is prevented from reaching large community audiences, it is reasonable to ask whether local people are receiving a balanced picture of events.

Too often, debate can become centred on labels rather than evidence. Terms such as 'misinformation', 'divisive' or 'harmful' should only be used where they can be supported by facts. If reporting is inaccurate, it should be corrected. If facts are disputed, they should be challenged with evidence. Robust debate is healthier than silent suppression.

Independent local journalism has become increasingly important as traditional local newsrooms have shrunk. Smaller publishers often report stories that might otherwise receive little attention, giving residents access to a broader range of information and perspectives.

Ultimately, Facebook groups have become powerful gatekeepers of local information. That influence brings responsibility. While moderators are free to manage their communities as they see fit, readers should also recognise that what appears in a Facebook feed is not necessarily the full picture of what is happening across Rochdale borough.

A healthy democracy depends on people having access to a range of lawful reporting and being trusted to reach their own conclusions.

articles.title: Low-flying helicopter heard across Rochdale as residents ask what happened
articles.excerpt: Residents across Rochdale reported hearing and seeing a helicopter flying unusually low over the borough on Monday evening, prompting widespread discussion on local social media.
articles.content_html:
A low-flying helicopter was heard and seen across several parts of Rochdale on Monday evening, with many residents taking to local social media groups to ask why the aircraft was circling over the borough.

Reports came from multiple neighbourhoods, with people describing the helicopter as flying lower than usual and remaining in the area for an extended period. The activity quickly prompted speculation online, with some residents wondering whether a major incident had taken place.

At the time of publication, neither Greater Manchester Police nor the National Police Air Service had announced a major incident linked to the helicopter, and no public statement had been issued explaining its deployment.

Police helicopters are routinely used to support officers on the ground across Greater Manchester. They may assist with searching for missing people, tracking suspects, providing aerial observations during ongoing incidents or supporting other emergency service operations. Not every deployment results in a public announcement, particularly where there is no wider risk to the public or where operational reasons prevent police from releasing information.

It is therefore not unusual for residents to notice the aircraft without an immediate explanation being made available.

Anyone who witnessed an emergency incident connected with the helicopter or has information that could assist police should contact Greater Manchester Police through the appropriate reporting channels. If there is an immediate threat to life or crime in progress, people should always dial 999.

Rochdale Daily will update this article if Greater Manchester Police or the National Police Air Service releases further information about Monday evening's deployment.

articles.title: Why are so many taxis in Heywood licensed in Wolverhampton and other areas?
articles.excerpt: Many private hire vehicles working in Heywood display licence plates issued by Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other distant councils. Here is why the practice is legal, why it remains controversial and when an offence may be committed.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Heywood have increasingly been asking the same question: why are so many taxis driving around the town registered in Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other places?

For many people, the sight of private hire vehicles displaying licences issued by councils hundreds of miles away raises concerns about who regulates them, whether they are operating legally and who is responsible if something goes wrong.

The issue has become controversial across England, with local authorities, taxi trade representatives and residents questioning whether the current licensing system gives councils enough control over the vehicles regularly working in their communities.

Why is it controversial?

The debate centres on cross-border licensing.

Since changes introduced under the Deregulation Act 2015, private hire vehicles are no longer expected to work primarily within the area that licensed them. As a result, a driver licensed by Wolverhampton City Council can legally spend most of the working day carrying passengers in Greater Manchester, provided the vehicle and driver comply with the law governing private hire bookings.

Critics argue that the system has weakened local oversight. Drivers may work almost exclusively in Greater Manchester despite being licensed by an authority many miles away, while local councils have less direct control over drivers they did not licence themselves.

Residents may also be unsure which authority they should contact if they wish to make a complaint. Enforcement can become more complicated when several licensing authorities are involved, while different councils may apply different licensing policies and standards.

These concerns have been raised by local authorities across England for several years, with many calling on the Government to reform private hire legislation and give councils greater control over vehicles operating regularly within their boundaries.

Does that mean these vehicles are operating illegally?

No. Although the system is controversial, simply seeing a vehicle licensed in Wolverhampton, Knowsley or another authority driving around Heywood does not mean it is breaking the law.

Private hire licensing works differently from the licensing of traditional taxis.

Unlike a hackney carriage, which can be hailed in the street or wait on an official taxi rank, a private hire vehicle must be pre-booked through a licensed private hire operator before the journey begins.

A Wolverhampton-licensed vehicle seen driving through Heywood could lawfully be travelling to collect a passenger who has already booked, dropping off a customer, waiting for its next booking through an operator or app, or returning from a previous fare.

The licence plate alone does not indicate whether the vehicle is acting lawfully.

When would it become an offence?

The law is much clearer if a private hire vehicle accepts work without a booking.

A private hire driver cannot legally accept passengers who flag the vehicle down in the street, wait on designated taxi ranks or carry passengers without a booking that has first been accepted by a licensed private hire operator.

Those activities are generally reserved for licensed hackney carriage taxis.

If residents witness a private hire vehicle picking up passengers without a booking, licensing officers can investigate whether an offence has been committed.

Who is responsible for enforcement?

One reason the issue generates debate is that responsibility can involve several organisations.

The council that issued the driver's licence retains important regulatory powers and can investigate complaints or suspend and revoke licences where appropriate.

Greater Manchester Police can deal with suspected criminal offences, while local licensing officers may carry out roadside inspections and joint enforcement operations with other authorities.

Many licensing authorities now share intelligence and work together to improve enforcement across council boundaries.

Why Wolverhampton?

Wolverhampton has become one of the country's largest private hire licensing authorities.

Over recent years it has processed applications from drivers across England, meaning many vehicles operating in towns and cities far from the West Midlands legitimately display Wolverhampton licence plates.

The same principle applies to vehicles licensed by authorities such as Knowsley and other councils outside Greater Manchester.

The bigger debate

The growing number of vehicles displaying out-of-area licences has become a national political issue.

Supporters of the current system argue that it provides flexibility for drivers, supports competition and allows passengers to access transport more easily, particularly through app-based booking services.

Critics believe councils should have greater powers over vehicles that spend most of their time working within their communities, regardless of where those vehicles and drivers were originally licensed.

Successive governments have considered reforms to taxi and private hire legislation, but cross-border private hire work remains lawful under the current framework.

What should residents know?

For anyone wondering why so many vehicles in Heywood display Wolverhampton, Knowsley or other out-of-area licence plates, the answer is that the law allows it.

Their presence alone is not evidence of illegal activity.

The important legal question is not where the vehicle is licensed, but whether it is operating as a genuine private hire vehicle, with every journey properly pre-booked through a licensed operator.

Where there is evidence that a private hire vehicle is accepting passengers without bookings or otherwise breaking licensing rules, those concerns can be investigated by the relevant licensing authority and, where appropriate, the police.
